work.title: The Life of King Henry the Fifth

scene.label: Act 3, Scene 7
scene.title: SCENE VII. The French camp, near Agincourt.

content.text: Enter the Constable of France, the Lord Rambures, Orleans, Dauphin with others.

lines.text: Tut! I have the best armour of the world.
lines.plainText: Tut I have the best armour of the world

lines.text: Would it were day!
lines.plainText: Would it were day

lines.text: You have an excellent armour; but let my horse have his due.
lines.plainText: You have an excellent armour but let my horse have his due

lines.text: It is the best horse of Europe.
lines.plainText: It is the best horse of Europe

lines.text: Will it never be morning?
lines.plainText: Will it never be morning

lines.text: My Lord of Orleans, and my Lord High Constable, you talk of horse and armour?
lines.plainText: My Lord of Orleans and my Lord High Constable you talk of horse and armour

lines.text: You are as well provided of both as any prince in the world.
lines.plainText: You are as well provided of both as any prince in the world

lines.text: What a long night is this! I will not change my horse with any that treads but on four pasterns. Ch'ha! He bounds from the earth, as if his entrails were hairs; le cheval volant, the Pegasus, qui a les narines de feu! When I bestride him, I soar, I am a hawk. He trots the air; the earth sings when he touches it; the basest horn of his hoof is more musical than the pipe of Hermes.
lines.plainText: What a long night is this I will not change my horse with any that treads but on four pasterns Ch'ha He bounds from the earth as if his entrails were hairs le cheval volant the Pegasus qui a les narines de feu When I bestride him I soar I am a hawk He trots the air the earth sings when he touches it the basest horn of his hoof is more musical than the pipe of Hermes

lines.text: He's of the colour of the nutmeg.
lines.plainText: He's of the colour of the nutmeg

lines.text: And of the heat of the ginger. It is a beast for Perseus. He is pure air and fire; and the dull elements of earth and water never appear in him, but only in patient stillness while his rider mounts him. He is indeed a horse, and all other jades you may call beasts.
lines.plainText: And of the heat of the ginger It is a beast for Perseus He is pure air and fire and the dull elements of earth and water never appear in him but only in patient stillness while his rider mounts him He is indeed a horse and all other jades you may call beasts

lines.text: Indeed, my lord, it is a most absolute and excellent horse.
lines.plainText: Indeed my lord it is a most absolute and excellent horse

lines.text: It is the prince of palfreys; his neigh is like the bidding of a monarch, and his countenance enforces homage.
lines.plainText: It is the prince of palfreys his neigh is like the bidding of a monarch and his countenance enforces homage

lines.text: No more, cousin.
lines.plainText: No more cousin

lines.text: Nay, the man hath no wit that cannot, from the rising of the lark to the lodging of the lamb, vary deserved praise on my palfrey. It is a theme as fluent as the sea; turn the sands into eloquent tongues, and my horse is argument for them all. 'Tis a subject for a sovereign to reason on, and for a sovereign's sovereign to ride on; and for the world, familiar to us and unknown, to lay apart their particular functions and wonder at him. I once writ a sonnet in his praise and began thus: "Wonder of nature,"—

lines.text: I have heard a sonnet begin so to one's mistress.
lines.plainText: I have heard a sonnet begin so to one's mistress

lines.text: Then did they imitate that which I compos'd to my courser, for my horse is my mistress.
lines.plainText: Then did they imitate that which I compos'd to my courser for my horse is my mistress

lines.text: Your mistress bears well.
lines.plainText: Your mistress bears well

lines.text: Me well; which is the prescript praise and perfection of a good and particular mistress.
lines.plainText: Me well which is the prescript praise and perfection of a good and particular mistress

lines.text: Nay, for methought yesterday your mistress shrewdly shook your back.
lines.plainText: Nay for methought yesterday your mistress shrewdly shook your back

lines.text: So perhaps did yours.
lines.plainText: So perhaps did yours

lines.text: Mine was not bridled.
lines.plainText: Mine was not bridled

lines.text: O then belike she was old and gentle; and you rode, like a kern of Ireland, your French hose off, and in your strait strossers.
lines.plainText: O then belike she was old and gentle and you rode like a kern of Ireland your French hose off and in your strait strossers

lines.text: You have good judgment in horsemanship.
lines.plainText: You have good judgment in horsemanship

lines.text: Be warn'd by me, then; they that ride so and ride not warily, fall into foul bogs. I had rather have my horse to my mistress.
lines.plainText: Be warn'd by me then they that ride so and ride not warily fall into foul bogs I had rather have my horse to my mistress

lines.text: I had as lief have my mistress a jade.
lines.plainText: I had as lief have my mistress a jade

lines.text: I tell thee, Constable, my mistress wears his own hair.
lines.plainText: I tell thee Constable my mistress wears his own hair

lines.text: I could make as true a boast as that, if I had a sow to my mistress.
lines.plainText: I could make as true a boast as that if I had a sow to my mistress

lines.text: "Le chien est retourné à son propre vomissement, et la truie lavée au bourbier." Thou mak'st use of anything.
lines.plainText: Le chien est retourn son propre vomissement et la truie lave au bourbier Thou mak'st use of anything

lines.text: Yet do I not use my horse for my mistress, or any such proverb so little kin to the purpose.
lines.plainText: Yet do I not use my horse for my mistress or any such proverb so little kin to the purpose

lines.text: My Lord Constable, the armour that I saw in your tent tonight, are those stars or suns upon it?
lines.plainText: My Lord Constable the armour that I saw in your tent tonight are those stars or suns upon it

lines.text: Stars, my lord.
lines.plainText: Stars my lord

lines.text: Some of them will fall tomorrow, I hope.
lines.plainText: Some of them will fall tomorrow I hope

lines.text: And yet my sky shall not want.
lines.plainText: And yet my sky shall not want

lines.text: That may be, for you bear a many superfluously, and 'twere more honour some were away.
lines.plainText: That may be for you bear a many superfluously and 'twere more honour some were away

lines.text: Even as your horse bears your praises; who would trot as well, were some of your brags dismounted.
lines.plainText: Even as your horse bears your praises who would trot as well were some of your brags dismounted

lines.text: Would I were able to load him with his desert! Will it never be day? I will trot tomorrow a mile, and my way shall be paved with English faces.
lines.plainText: Would I were able to load him with his desert Will it never be day I will trot tomorrow a mile and my way shall be paved with English faces

lines.text: I will not say so, for fear I should be fac'd out of my way. But I would it were morning; for I would fain be about the ears of the English.
lines.plainText: I will not say so for fear I should be fac'd out of my way But I would it were morning for I would fain be about the ears of the English

lines.text: Who will go to hazard with me for twenty prisoners?
lines.plainText: Who will go to hazard with me for twenty prisoners

lines.text: You must first go yourself to hazard, ere you have them.
lines.plainText: You must first go yourself to hazard ere you have them

lines.text: 'Tis midnight; I'll go arm myself.
lines.plainText: 'Tis midnight I'll go arm myself

lines.text: The Dauphin longs for morning.
lines.plainText: The Dauphin longs for morning

lines.text: He longs to eat the English.
lines.plainText: He longs to eat the English

lines.text: I think he will eat all he kills.
lines.plainText: I think he will eat all he kills

lines.text: By the white hand of my lady, he's a gallant prince.
lines.plainText: By the white hand of my lady he's a gallant prince

lines.text: Swear by her foot that she may tread out the oath.
lines.plainText: Swear by her foot that she may tread out the oath

lines.text: He is simply the most active gentleman of France.
lines.plainText: He is simply the most active gentleman of France

lines.text: Doing is activity; and he will still be doing.
lines.plainText: Doing is activity and he will still be doing

lines.text: He never did harm, that I heard of.
lines.plainText: He never did harm that I heard of

lines.text: Nor will do none tomorrow. He will keep that good name still.
lines.plainText: Nor will do none tomorrow He will keep that good name still

lines.text: I know him to be valiant.
lines.plainText: I know him to be valiant

lines.text: I was told that by one that knows him better than you.
lines.plainText: I was told that by one that knows him better than you

lines.text: What's he?
lines.plainText: What's he

lines.text: Marry, he told me so himself; and he said he car'd not who knew it.
lines.plainText: Marry he told me so himself and he said he car'd not who knew it

lines.text: He needs not; it is no hidden virtue in him.
lines.plainText: He needs not it is no hidden virtue in him

lines.text: By my faith, sir, but it is; never anybody saw it but his lackey. 'Tis a hooded valour; and when it appears, it will bate.
lines.plainText: By my faith sir but it is never anybody saw it but his lackey 'Tis a hooded valour and when it appears it will bate

lines.text: "Ill will never said well."
lines.plainText: Ill will never said well

lines.text: I will cap that proverb with "There is flattery in friendship."
lines.plainText: I will cap that proverb with There is flattery in friendship

lines.text: And I will take up that with "Give the devil his due."
lines.plainText: And I will take up that with Give the devil his due

lines.text: Well plac'd. There stands your friend for the devil; have at the very eye of that proverb with "A pox of the devil."
lines.plainText: Well plac'd There stands your friend for the devil have at the very eye of that proverb with A pox of the devil

lines.text: You are the better at proverbs, by how much "A fool's bolt is soon shot."
lines.plainText: You are the better at proverbs by how much A fool's bolt is soon shot

lines.text: 'Tis not the first time you were overshot.
lines.plainText: 'Tis not the first time you were overshot

lines.text: My Lord High Constable, the English lie within fifteen hundred paces of your tents.
lines.plainText: My Lord High Constable the English lie within fifteen hundred paces of your tents

lines.text: Who hath measur'd the ground?
lines.plainText: Who hath measur'd the ground

lines.text: The Lord Grandpré.
lines.plainText: The Lord Grandpr

lines.text: A valiant and most expert gentleman. Would it were day! Alas, poor Harry of England, he longs not for the dawning as we do.
lines.plainText: A valiant and most expert gentleman Would it were day Alas poor Harry of England he longs not for the dawning as we do

lines.text: What a wretched and peevish fellow is this King of England, to mope with his fat-brain'd followers so far out of his knowledge!
lines.plainText: What a wretched and peevish fellow is this King of England to mope with his fatbrain'd followers so far out of his knowledge

lines.text: If the English had any apprehension, they would run away.
lines.plainText: If the English had any apprehension they would run away

lines.text: That they lack; for if their heads had any intellectual armour, they could never wear such heavy head-pieces.
lines.plainText: That they lack for if their heads had any intellectual armour they could never wear such heavy headpieces

lines.text: That island of England breeds very valiant creatures. Their mastiffs are of unmatchable courage.
lines.plainText: That island of England breeds very valiant creatures Their mastiffs are of unmatchable courage

lines.text: Foolish curs, that run winking into the mouth of a Russian bear and have their heads crush'd like rotten apples! You may as well say, that's a valiant flea that dare eat his breakfast on the lip of a lion.
lines.plainText: Foolish curs that run winking into the mouth of a Russian bear and have their heads crush'd like rotten apples You may as well say that's a valiant flea that dare eat his breakfast on the lip of a lion

lines.text: Just, just; and the men do sympathize with the mastiffs in robustious and rough coming on, leaving their wits with their wives; and then, give them great meals of beef and iron and steel, they will eat like wolves and fight like devils.

lines.text: Ay, but these English are shrewdly out of beef.
lines.plainText: Ay but these English are shrewdly out of beef

lines.text: Then shall we find tomorrow they have only stomachs to eat and none to fight. Now is it time to arm. Come, shall we about it?
